title: Why Unpacking a Standard Matters
description: Coverage isn't the same as teaching. Before planning a single lesson, unpack the standard so you know exactly what students need to know and do — the work below the surface that any good lesson plan is built on.
howTo:
Read the full standard slowly before opening a textbook chapter or resource.
Break the standard into the pieces students will actually need: the skill, the content, the academic vocabulary, and the depth of thinking required.
Name what's explicit in the standard's wording and what's implicit — the background knowledge or vocabulary the standard assumes but doesn't state.
Build a rough hierarchy of skills — what has to come first, second, and last — before choosing a single activity or worksheet.
Only after this groundwork, move to selecting engaging learning experiences and aligned resources.
example: Before teaching a persuasive-writing standard, a teacher lists the skill (constructing an argument), the content (a real issue students care about), the vocabulary (claim, counterclaim, rebuttal), and the depth of thinking required — then picks activities and mentor texts that match, instead of starting with "a persuasive essay unit" and working backward.
sourceName: Edutopia — "Common Core Big Idea 3: Standards Must Be Unpacked" (McTighe & Wiggins)

title: Reading a Standard: Verb, Content, and Cognitive Demand
description: Every standard hides two things in plain sight: a verb that names the skill and a noun that names the content it applies to. Learning to see both — and the thinking level they demand — is the first move in unpacking any standard.
howTo:
Underline the verb(s) in the standard — this is the skill students must be able to do.
Circle the noun(s) and modifiers — this is the content or concept the skill applies to.
Sort the verb by rigor: is it asking students to recall, apply, analyze, or create?
List the baseline understandings and prerequisite skills the verb-noun combination implies, even if the standard doesn't state them directly.
Record the dissected standard somewhere your team can see it before planning lessons or assessments.
example: For a standard that reads "cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis," the verb is cite/support (skill) and the noun is textual evidence/analysis (content) — which tells a teacher students need explicit instruction in selecting relevant evidence, not just reading the text.
sourceName: Education Week — "Unwrapping the Standards: A Simple Way to Deconstruct Learning Outcomes" (Larry Ainsworth)

title: Costa's Levels of Thinking and Your Standards
description: Costa's Levels of Thinking (Art Costa, popularized through AVID) sorts thinking into three levels: Gathering (Level 1 — on the page), Processing (Level 2 — between the lines), and Applying (Level 3 — beyond the text). Naming the level a standard actually asks for tells you what to teach, what to ask, and what evidence of learning to look for. It's the same job Webb's DOK does, but with a simpler map that students and teachers can share.
howTo:
Find the verb in the standard, then read what comes after it — the surrounding language is what usually sets the level, not the verb alone.
Sort the demand into one of Costa's three levels: Level 1 Gathering (identify, list, describe, define), Level 2 Processing (compare, infer, explain, analyze, classify), or Level 3 Applying (evaluate, judge, predict, hypothesize, defend, design).
Watch for phrases that automatically raise the level. "Cite evidence" or "support with evidence" pushes toward Level 2 or 3. "Predict what would happen if…", "design a…", "defend a position" — those are Level 3, no matter what verb starts the sentence.
Match your "I can" statement to the standard's level. If the standard is Level 3, the "I can" verb should be Level 3 too — "I can evaluate…and defend with evidence," not "I can list…".
Write question stems at the standard's level and use them for bell-ringers, exit tickets, and discussion. AVID's own handouts publish sentence starters for each level.
example: "Identify the steps of the water cycle" is Level 1 Gathering — the answer is on the page. "Compare evaporation and condensation and explain what the differences mean for weather" is Level 2 Processing — students are between the lines. "Design a solution that reduces evaporation loss in an agricultural setting and defend your design with evidence" is Level 3 Applying — students go beyond the text.
videoTitle: How to Write Effective Questions with Costa's Levels of Thinking
sourceName: AVID Open Access — "Costa's Levels of Thinking" (student handout, PDF)

title: From Standard to Student-Friendly “I Can” Targets
description: Students can't hit a target they can't see. Translating a standard's academic language into a clear "I can" statement gives students something concrete to aim for and self-assess against.
howTo:
Agree on the learning target embedded in the standard before writing anything student-facing.
Divide a big standard into smaller, single-focus components rather than one sprawling target.
Write each target in first person, starting with "I can," using a measurable verb (solve, identify, write, explain) instead of a vague one (understand, know, learn).
Sequence multiple "I can" statements in the order students will actually meet them across the unit.
Post or share the target where students see it before the lesson starts, so they know what they're working toward and how they'll show it.
example: "Students will evaluate how literary elements impact theme, mood, and tone using textual evidence" becomes "I can explain how an author's choice of setting or conflict shapes a story's mood, and back it up with a quote from the text."
videoTitle: How to Unpack Standards: A Practical Guide for Educators
sourceName: Solution Tree — "Crafting I Can Statements: A Practice Worth Pursuing" (Thomas W. Many)

title: Building a Learning Progression From a Standard
description: A single standard rarely stands alone — it sits on a staircase of prerequisite skills. Naming that staircase tells you where to start instruction for the students in front of you, not just where the standard lands on grade level.
howTo:
Identify the explicit skills and knowledge the standard states directly.
Name the implicit prerequisite skills the standard assumes but doesn't spell out.
Look at the standard one or two grade levels below and above to see how the skill develops over time.
Use the progression to locate where an individual student currently is, not just where the grade-level standard sits.
Treat the progression as an instructional tool for feedback and intervention — not a rigid pacing guide or script.
example: Before a 7th-grade proportional-reasoning standard, a teacher checks the 6th-grade ratio standard below it and confirms most students can already represent a ratio before layering on proportional word problems.
sourceName: Compass PD — "Learning Progressions: From Standards to Student Learning" (Dr. Sherri Lorton)

title: Making the Standard Relevant to Students
description: “Why do we have to learn this?” is a real question, not a complaint. Connecting a standard to something students already care about — before you teach the skill — makes the standard worth engaging with.
howTo:
Ask what this standard connects to outside the classroom — a real problem, a community issue, or something students already notice.
Frame the purpose before the task: tell students why this skill matters before you hand them the assignment.
Where possible, give students a genuine audience or stakeholder for their work, not just a grade.
Sustain the relevance through the whole task, not just a one-time hook at the start of the unit.
Write a short relevancy statement you can say out loud in under a minute before starting the lesson.
example: Instead of announcing "today we're writing persuasive essays," a teacher has students research a real school policy they want changed and write to the actual decision-maker who could change it.
videoTitle: Solving Real-World Problems: Bringing Authentic Context to Learning
sourceName: ASCD Educational Leadership — "Designing Relevant Learning" (Doug Fisher and Nancy Frey)

title: Oklahoma Standards in Action: Reading/ELA
description: A real Oklahoma Academic Standard for English Language Arts, unpacked step by step using the moves from Chapters 1–6.
howTo:
Skill (verb): evaluate — using textual evidence to support an analysis, not just identify or list the literary elements.
Content (noun): the impact of literary elements — setting, plot structure, conflict, characters, characterization, point of view, and archetypes — on theme, mood, and/or tone.
Costa level: Strategic Thinking (Costa Level 3) — evaluating the impact of an element and supporting it with evidence goes well beyond simply naming the element.
Prerequisite skills: students must already be able to identify each literary element by name and locate relevant textual evidence before they can evaluate its impact.
Student-friendly target: "I can show how a specific literary element — like conflict or point of view — shapes a story's mood or theme, and prove it with a quote from the text."
example: A teacher pulls a passage where the point-of-view narrator is unreliable, has students first identify the archetype and point of view (recall), then evaluate how that choice specifically creates suspense or irony in the mood (the actual Costa Level 3 demand of the standard).
sourceName: Oklahoma State Department of Education — 2021 Oklahoma Academic Standards for English Language Arts
subject: Reading/ELA
standardText: Students will evaluate how literary elements impact theme, mood, and/or tone, using textual evidence: setting; plot structure (e.g., foreshadowing, flashback, in media res); conflict (i.e., internal, external); characters (e.g., protagonist, antagonist); characterization (i.e., direct, indirect); point of view (e.g., narrator reliability); archetypes.

title: Oklahoma Standards in Action: Math
description: A real Oklahoma Academic Standard for Mathematics, unpacked step by step — and one that comes with its own built-in learning progression.
howTo:
Skill (verb): understand functions as descriptions of covariation — how two related quantities change together.
Content (noun): real-world and mathematical problems where one quantity depends on another.
Costa level: the parent standard is conceptual (Skills & Concepts, Costa Level 2), but its five objectives climb in demand — from distinguishing relations and functions (Costa Level 1) up through interpreting whether a graph is discrete or continuous (Costa Level 2–3).
Prerequisite skills: the standard's own objectives are already a built-in sequence — identify dependent/independent variables and domain/range before writing function notation or reading a piecewise graph.
Student-friendly target: "I can tell whether a relationship between two changing quantities is a function, and use function notation to describe how one depends on the other."
example: A teacher starts with A1.F.1.1 (distinguishing relations from functions using simple input-output tables) before ever asking students to write a function in notation (A1.F.1.3) — following the standard's own objective order as the lesson sequence.
sourceName: Oklahoma State Department of Education — 2022 Oklahoma Academic Standards for Mathematics
subject: Math
standardText: Understand functions as descriptions of covariation (how related quantities vary together) in real-world and mathematical problems. A1.F.1.1 Distinguish between relations and functions. A1.F.1.2 Identify the dependent variable, independent variable, domain and range given a function, equation, or graph. Identify restrictions on the domain and range in mathematical models. A1.F.1.3 Write linear functions, using function notation, to represent mathematical models. A1.F.1.4 Read and interpret the linear piecewise function, given a graph modeling a situation. A1.F.1.5 Interpret graphs as being discrete or continuous.

title: Oklahoma Standards in Action: Science
description: A real Oklahoma Academic Standard for Science, unpacked step by step — including the explicit assessment boundary the standard sets for itself.
howTo:
Skill (verb): construct an explanation based on evidence — a three-dimensional performance expectation, not a fact to memorize.
Content (noun): how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through specialized cells.
Costa level: Strategic Thinking (Costa Level 3) — constructing and justifying an evidence-based explanation is well above simply recalling that "DNA makes proteins."
Prerequisite skills and boundary: students need a conceptual grasp of transcription and translation — but the standard's own clarification statement explicitly excludes testing on specific cell/tissue types, whole-body systems, or the biochemistry of protein synthesis, so don't over-teach past that line.
Student-friendly target: "I can explain, using evidence, how the sequence of DNA determines the proteins a cell builds — without needing to memorize every step of protein synthesis."
example: A teacher has students construct a written explanation connecting a DNA mutation to a changed protein and a resulting trait, using a provided evidence set — stopping at the conceptual link the standard asks for, not drilling amino-acid biochemistry the standard explicitly excludes.
sourceName: Oklahoma State Department of Education — 2020 Oklahoma Academic Standards for Science
subject: Science
standardText: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells. Clarification Statement: Emphasis is on the conceptual understanding that the sequence of nucleotides in DNA determines the amino acid sequence of proteins through the processes of transcription and translation. Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include identification of specific cell or tissue types, whole body systems, specific protein structures and functions, or the biochemistry of protein synthesis.

title: Oklahoma Standards in Action: Social Studies
description: A real Oklahoma Academic Standard for Social Studies, unpacked step by step — showing how one umbrella verb can sit on top of several lower-demand component verbs.
howTo:
Skill (umbrella verb): evaluate — sitting on top of four lower-Costa-level component verbs: describe, explain, trace, and describe again.
Content (noun): the rise and reforms of Populism and the Progressive Movement, including democratic-process reforms, William Jennings Bryan's influence, the 16th and 17th Amendments, and antitrust legislation.
Costa level: the umbrella "evaluate" sits at Strategic Thinking (Costa Level 3), while the four lettered components sit lower (Costa Level 1–2: describe, explain, trace) — they're the building blocks the evaluation is built on.
Prerequisite skills: students need working vocabulary — direct primary, initiative, referendum, recall, trust, monopoly — before they can meaningfully evaluate whether the reforms worked.
Student-friendly target: "I can explain how specific Progressive Era reforms — like the 17th Amendment or antitrust laws — tried to fix the problems of Populism and industrial power, and judge how well they worked."
example: A teacher has students first complete the four lettered components as stations (describe democratic reforms, explain Bryan's influence, trace the 16th/17th Amendments, describe antitrust acts) before asking the culminating Costa Level 3 question: did these reforms actually fix what they were meant to fix?
sourceName: Oklahoma State Department of Education — Oklahoma Academic Standards for Social Studies (7.10.26)
subject: Social Studies
standardText: Evaluate the rise and reforms of Populism and the Progressive Movement. A. Describe how democratic processes (e.g., direct primary, initiative petition, referendum, recall) intended to limit political corruption by making politicians and lawmaking more immediately responsive to the people. B. Explain the impact of William Jennings Bryan and his Cross of Gold message on the political landscape. C. Trace the series of events leading to and the effects of the 16th and 17th Amendments to the Constitution of the United States of America. D. Describe how the rise of trusts and monopolies impacted consumers and workers, prompting government's response with the Sherman and Clayton Antitrust Acts.

title: Planning What to Do
description: Once a standard is unpacked, the next question is what you'll actually do in the room to teach it — chosen backward from the standard, not from whatever activity is easiest to grab.
howTo:
Identify and document the standard(s) driving this lesson or unit before choosing an activity.
Plan backward from the standard: decide the end evidence of learning before picking the instructional tasks.
Choose real content and purposeful activities that connect directly to the standard's skill and content, not just an entertaining task.
Differentiate access to the same standard rather than lowering the standard itself.
Make sure every planned activity ties back to at least one success criterion drawn from the standard.
example: Planning a novel study, a teacher selects vocabulary, fluency, theme, and character-comparison activities directly tied to the unit's standards — and builds in scaffolded, differentiated access to the complex text rather than swapping in an easier book for struggling readers.
videoTitle: Planning a Standards-Based Lesson or Unit

title: Planning How You'll Check for Learning
description: You can't wait for the unit test to find out who's got it. Planning quick, low-stakes checks throughout the lesson tells you who to reteach and who's ready to move on — in time to actually do something about it.
howTo:
Build in quick, low-stakes checks throughout the lesson, not just at the end of the unit.
Use a mix of checks: observation, mini whiteboards, quick writes, discussion protocols, and self-assessment.
Use what you see to adjust teaching in the moment — reteach, regroup, or move on.
Make checks visible to students too, so they can see their own progress toward the target.
Keep checks ungraded where possible, so students take genuine risks instead of playing it safe.
example: A teaching team uses random student selection, a Learning Intentions Wall, mini whiteboards, and traffic-light self-reflections across a lesson — adjusting the next activity based on how many whiteboards show the wrong answer.

title: Sequencing the Learning Progression
description: The prerequisite staircase you named while unpacking the standard now becomes the actual order of your unit — simplest and most concrete first, most independent application last.
howTo:
Lay out the prerequisite skills identified during standards unpacking across the unit's weeks or days.
Sequence from the simplest, most concrete skills toward the most complex, most independent application of the standard.
Use the sequence to plan differentiated entry points for students who are behind or ahead of grade level.
Revisit the sequence mid-unit and adjust based on what your check-for-learning data actually shows.
Treat the sequence as a living plan, not a locked pacing calendar.
example: A teacher plans five complexity levels across a two-week unit — beginning, developing, approaching, applying, extending — so students entering at different starting points all have a next step instead of one single, one-size-fits-all lesson each day.

title: Planning Backward-Designed Assessments
description: Design the proof of mastery before you design the lessons that lead to it. Backward design keeps every activity pointed at the same target the standard actually asks for.
howTo:
Before planning any lesson, decide what evidence would prove a student has mastered the standard.
Design the summative assessment first — the task or test that will provide that evidence.
Check the assessment against the standard's Costa level so a low-level quiz isn't used to assess a high-Costa-level standard.
Use the six facets of understanding — explanation, interpretation, application, perspective, empathy, self-knowledge — to check that an assessment goes beyond recall.
Only after the assessment is designed, plan the lessons and activities that prepare students for it.
example: A persuasive-writing unit is scored against an authentic argument-writing rubric that checks for a defensible claim and addressed counterclaims — not a five-paragraph structure checklist — because that's the actual evidence the standard calls for.
videoTitle: Jay McTighe on the Backward Design Framework
sourceName: ASCD — "Understanding by Design® Framework" white paper (Jay McTighe and Grant Wiggins)
